title: Blessing of the animals (4 October)
hookLine: on Francis's day, churches bless pets and farm animals

lines: A LINE IN THE PARKING LOT.
A GOLDFISH IN A JAM JAR.
cards: A church parking lot on a Sunday afternoon. A line waits in the sun: a spaniel on a red leash, a boy with a goldfish in a jam jar, an elderly woman with a cat that clearly did not agree to come, a tortoise in a shoebox.
At the front, a minister or priest bends to each one, says a few words, sometimes sprinkles a little water. The cat objects. The spaniel tries to lick the prayer book.
It happens on or near the feast of Francis of Assisi, who called the creatures his brothers and sisters. Today, the Blessing of the animals.

teach.h: GOD SAW THAT IT WAS GOOD.
teach.b: Why bless a goldfish? The answer starts on the Bible's first page. In Genesis, on the sixth day, God says, "Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind."
And the refrain comes again: God saw that it was good. Animals aren't scenery in the story. They're made and called good before any human is there to use them.
Now a detail in the Hebrew.

The words for living creature are nefesh chayah. In the next chapter, when God breathes into the first human, "man became a living soul," and the Hebrew uses the same phrase. English splits it into creature and soul.
Hebrew gives humans and animals the same two words. The Bible keeps the animals in God's care. After the flood, God's promise is made with Noah "and with every living creature that is with you."
A psalm says, "O LORD, thou preservest man and beast."
And Jesus says a sparrow, sold cheap, "shall not fall on the ground without your Father." Then Francis.

His early biographers tell of him calling animals brother and sister, and a story in the Little Flowers tells of a wolf that troubled the town of Gubbio, whom Francis called brother wolf and made peace with.
Whatever you make of the wolf, the habit is the point. Not it. Not livestock.
Brother. So a blessing of the animals isn't a joke service, even with the cat yowling. It says out loud what Genesis said first: this living creature is God's, and it is good.

how: On or near the feast of Francis of Assisi, some Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches hold a blessing of the animals, where people bring pets or farm animals and a priest or minister blesses each one.

games.q: you're Francis. a wolf has been troubling the town of Gubbio, and everyone is afraid. what do you do?
o: help the town hunt it down.
go out to meet it, call it brother wolf and make peace.
tell the town to move away.
games.why: the Little Flowers tells that Francis went out, called it brother wolf, and made peace between the wolf and the town.

practice: If there's an animal near you, a dog at your feet, a cat on the sofa, watch it for a while and notice how it breathes; if not, bring to mind one you've known and loved.
If you pray, thank God for that creature or ask a blessing on it in your own words; if you don't, just watch, or remember, with care and thanks.

wordCard.voice: Nefesh chayah. Hebrew for a living creature, the same two words the Bible uses for the first human, and for every animal blessed on this day.

orig.note: Hebrew, Genesis 1:24: a living creature. the same words describe the first human in Genesis 2:7.
